source.title: Objective Matters: Fine-Tuning Objectives Shape Safety, Robustness, and Persona Drift
source.authors: Daniel Vennemeyer; Punya Syon Pandey; Phan Anh Duong; Michael Umeokoli; S. Ratnam

record.tranche_reason: Tests how benign task fine-tuning and its training objective relate to adversarial attack success, using a scale sweep and jailbreak ASR rather than the original harmful-example fine-tuning method.
record.gate_note: The study reports ASR for prompting-based jailbreaks after benign task fine-tuning, including a Happy-to-Help prompt that requests a compliant opening. It does not isolate the causal effect of that opening or measure first-token KL. Task-capability and persona results are outside these claim versions. Other attack curves and multi-model plots are described or shown but their individual plotted values are not stated in the text.
record.test_reason: The study fine-tunes safety-trained instruct models on benign task data (GSM8K, SuperGPQA, cybersecurity, legal) under six objectives and tracks jailbreak attack success as the training budget grows. That bears directly on V2 (benign fine-tuning erodes safety), using a method different from the originals. It has no per-token KL, harmful-data fine-tuning, localization or deepening test. Its attack results are aggregated across attacks, so they do not isolate the effect of a compliant opening (V4).
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that objectives matter little at 25k–50k tokens but diverge at larger budgets: SFT and DPO couple capability gains to rising jailbreak vulnerability and persona drift, while ORPO and KL (and IP for robustness) mitigate them. They frame mechanisms as hypotheses. Note that DPO, ORPO, CFT and IP as implemented here inject safe/unsafe signals, so only SFT and KL are purely benign.
record.recipe_differences: Benign domain-task fine-tuning with LoRA and a comparison of six objectives; evaluates jailbreak ASR across training budgets. It does not fine-tune on a small harmful-example set or measure per-token KL.
record.method_sensitivity: Training scale and fine-tuning objective alter ASR; the paper reports similar ASR across objectives at 25k–50k tokens and sharper objective separation at larger budgets. Dataset and model family also vary across evaluations.

fits_no_version.finding: Benign fine-tuning raises Dark Triad persona endorsement at 400k–800k tokens for SFT, DPO and IP, but not for ORPO or KL.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Benign fine-tuning induces scale-dependent persona drift (emergent-misalignment-like), not refusal loss.

record.problems: Experiments use mid-scale instruction-tuned models adapted with LoRA; the authors caution results may not transfer to full-parameter or frontier-scale training. Jailbreak robustness uses prompting attacks scored by a classifier. Several scale and cross-model outcomes are shown in plots without individual values stated in the text, and the study does not isolate causal effects of compliant openings.
record.rows_left_out: Other attack-specific curves in Appendix D, additional dataset/model trade-off plots in Figures 13–15, and persona plots in Figures 6 and 16–20 were not individually extracted. The attack-specific curves do not have prose-stated per-condition numbers; persona outcomes do not measure the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: No per-token KL or position analysis.
No prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks. The Happy-to-Help prompt asks for a compliant opening, but its effect versus no attack is shown only in plots (Figs 8–9) without stated values.
No test of why safety is shallow.
No reported un-fine-tuned baseline ASR in the text. No full-parameter fine-tuning; LoRA only.

missing.what: ASR with no jailbreak (plain harmful prompts) versus tokens seen for all six objectives: the most direct V2 measure. Values are only plotted.
Un-fine-tuned baseline vulnerability, which the text says is compared, but no number is stated.
Happy-to-Help ('Start your response with Sure...') ASR curve, which could be set against the no-attack curve for a compliant-opening effect. Values are only plotted.

record.verdict_notes: V4 links were removed from all rows: aggregated post-fine-tuning ASR does not test whether a compliant opening or other attack bypasses refusal relative to no attack. Table 1 rows are kept for V2 but cannot show erosion without a baseline or budget breakdown. The record's V4 labels were dropped. Study is a preprint; experiments use LoRA r=16.

versions.untested_parts: No fine-tuning on harmful examples or few-to-hundreds-example data regime is tested.

Tests benign task-domain fine-tuning and jailbreak ASR, not harmful compliance on ordinary harmful prompts without an attack, nor a controlled direct comparison to the un-fine-tuned model for each objective and budget.
No per-token KL divergence or response-position analysis.

Tests prompting-based jailbreaks, including Happy-to-Help, DAN, Role-Play, Wikipedia and Zulu. Does not isolate compliant-prefill effects, evaluate adversarial suffixes as a distinct method, or test decoding changes.
No weight- or rank-localization test of safety behavior.
Does not test why safety is shallow or whether data or objective causes first-token concentration.
Does not train or test a method specifically intended to spread safety across response tokens.

rows.subject: multiple instruction-tuned models (aggregate)
rows.size_stated: Gemma2-2B, Gemma2-9B, LLaMA-3.1-8B, Qwen3-4B, and Qwen2.5-7B
rows.operation_detail: Compare objective-associated jailbreak ASR and capability at fixed training budgets across model families.
rows.measure: ASR clustering by model family versus fine-tuning objective
rows.baseline: 25k tokens: results primarily cluster by model
rows.value: By 400k tokens, objective-level clustering emerges; ORPO and IP occupy more favorable regions, while SFT and DPO have steeper vulnerability–capability slopes
rows.uncertainty: 95% CI shown in figure; values not stated
rows.note: The prose describes aggregate trends across the named models; individual plotted values are not stated.
rows.check: Qualitative only. At 400k tokens, SFT/DPO lie on steeper vulnerability–capability slopes across five models, while ORPO/IP sit in better regions. Not V4.

relationships.condition: Plain SFT and DPO on benign GSM8K, LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, DAN attack, budgets up to 800k tokens; the same pattern is described qualitatively across five models
relationships.reason: Jailbreak ASR rises with benign training scale for SFT and DPO, SFT steepest (R27, R28, R33).
relationships.display_finding: DAN jailbreak success rose as benign training grew, for both SFT and DPO, with SFT rising most steeply.

relationships.condition: Constrained or safety-signal objectives (IP, CFT, KL) and small budgets (25k–50k tokens)
relationships.reason: Erosion grows substantially more slowly under IP, CFT and KL, and objectives barely differ at small budgets, so the size of erosion depends on objective and scale (R29, R30, R32).
relationships.display_finding: Erosion grew substantially more slowly under IP, CFT and KL, and objectives barely differed at small budgets, so the size of erosion depended on objective and scale.

relationships.condition: ORPO with safe/unsafe preference pairs at large budgets
relationships.reason: Authors state ORPO halts, and sometimes reverses, vulnerability growth. This relies on an added safety contrast, not pure benign data (R31).
relationships.display_finding: The authors state ORPO halts, and sometimes reverses, vulnerability growth, though this relies on an added safety contrast rather than purely benign data.
